claim: Real execution output (unit tests, error messages) is what makes a debug loop work; without it the same loop gains little and can lose. Chen: TransCoder GPT-4 +13.1 with tests vs about +1 without; Codex MBPP simple feedback 61.4 to 57.6 without execution.
agent_test: Same model, same revise prompt, same token cap: arm A sees real test/run output, arm B gets only a prompt to check its answer. Compare solve rate.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction (no outside signal) does not improve reasoning and often lowers it. GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two rounds. Self-Refine on math: GPT-4 92.9 to 93.1.
agent_test: Run revise-without-evidence versus no revise at equal tokens; expect no gain, and count correct-to-wrong flips.

claim: Reported self-correction gains were often inflated by oracle labels used as the stop signal. Corrected numbers: oracle GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0; without oracle they fall. A loop with no reliable stop signal degrades (Reflexion no-tests 0.52 vs base 0.60).
agent_test: Never let the scaffold stop on a label the agent could not have in deployment; score stop decisions with a held-out check.

claim: At equal compute, self-repair beats plain resampling only slightly or not at all. GPT-4 APPS: 10 initial + 1 repair each = 1.05x pass@20; 2 initial + 10 repairs each = 0.97x. Only GPT-4 benefits significantly on APPS. Chen reports the opposite on Spider (debug 1 greedy = 16 samples), but counts samples not tokens and uses execution feedback. Gap search 2026-10-26: at matched calls BESTER shows plain repair often below sampling (DeepSeek APPS 57.54 sampling vs 53.67 repair); small frozen models: blind resampling beat bare-code retry by +18 net unlocks and tied code+facts; CodeMonkeys: equal-cost serial and parallel configurations reach similar coverage after the first few iterations. No matched test exists for a modern reasoning model.
agent_test: Equal-token three-arm test: best-of-N, repair-after-test, mixed. Report in pass@tokens, not pass@samples.

claim: Feedback quality is the bottleneck of self-repair. GPT-4 repairing with its own explanation 33.3% vs 52.6% with expert human explanation (16 participants, 40 programs); weaker coders do better with GPT-4 feedback than with their own.
agent_test: Swap the explanation step: same model's own diagnosis versus a stronger-model or human diagnosis, equal repair budget. If the gap is large, spend tokens on diagnosis.

claim: Finding the first wrong step is the hard part; fixing it is easier. Best model (GPT-4) locates the mistake step in only 52.87 overall on BIG-Bench Mistake; given the true step, backtracking raises originally wrong traces by +18 to +44 points, a random step by +5 to +21. With the true location, originally correct traces still lose up to 11 points.
agent_test: Add an explicit operator that names the first wrong step with evidence before any rewrite; measure localisation accuracy on planted errors.

claim: Showing real runtime variable values per basic block (LDB) beats model-simulated traces by small margins. HumanEval GPT-3.5 seed 73.8: LDB 82.9 vs Self-Debug 81.1; StarCoder Self-Debug -0.6, LDB +0.6. Authors' own comparison and setup.
agent_test: Let the agent insert print or probe statements and read real values vs only reading code; equal tokens.

claim: Rubber-duck style code explanation gives a modest gain when tests are absent: Spider Codex 81.3 to 84.1 (+2.8), GPT-3.5 +1.1, GPT-4 +0.4; no gain for GPT-3.5 on TransCoder. Model explanations of faults are often wrong (AutoFL: about 20% accurate). Re-opened AutoFL: 20% of 300 explanations accurate, 56.7% of bugs had at least one accurate one; the paper has no no-explanation arm, so explanation is not isolated from re-reading.
agent_test: Explain-then-fix vs fix directly at equal tokens, on tasks with no executable check.

claim: Nearly all the benefit of self-debugging arrives in the first turn on Spider (later turns add within 0.1%), but LDB kept improving to 10 iterations on HumanEval. Evidence conflicts on how many rounds are worth paying for. More evidence of early flattening: debug-gym says the final few rewrites bring virtually no value; S* picks 2 debug rounds; CodeMonkeys says the first few serial iterations carry the gain.
agent_test: Sweep round cap 1,2,3,5 at equal total tokens and plot the marginal gain per round.

claim: Debug loops repair small slips (missing WHERE, DISTINCT, wrong JOIN; 62-69% output mismatch), while unresolved agent runs are dominated by wrong or over-narrow implementations (52%) and flawed reasoning (about 65%). Loops fix near-misses, not wrong designs. TRAJEVAL (16,758 trajectories, 7 models): on SWE-agent Verified, 56.9% of failures across all models (64-69% for the five stronger models) reach and edit the right function and still fail (Edit-Quality bucket); of those, overwriting a correct edit (coherence collapse) is 39.7% (22.6% of all failures) and a wrong branch point 18.6%.
agent_test: Tag each failure as slip versus wrong design; test whether an explicit abandon-this-approach operator helps on wrong-design cases.
audit_note: TRAJEVAL's 56.9% is the weighted average across all seven models on SWE-agent (Verified, 1,607 failures), not 'strong models'; for the five strong models the Edit-Quality share is 64-69%. Other numbers (Chen 61.9/69.2%, 52.0%, ~65%, 39.7%/22.6%, 18.6%) check out.
claim_before_audit: Debug loops repair small slips (missing WHERE, DISTINCT, wrong JOIN; 62-69% output mismatch), while unresolved agent runs are dominated by wrong or over-narrow implementations (52%) and flawed reasoning (about 65%). Loops fix near-misses, not wrong designs. TRAJEVAL (16,758 trajectories): for strong models 56.9% of SWE-agent failures reach the right function and still fail; of those, overwriting a correct edit is 39.7% (22.6% of all failures) and a wrong branch point 18.6%.

claim: Self-generated tests are unreliable as the sole judge of success. Reflexion MBPP: 16.3% false positives, so pass@1 fell 80.1 to 77.1 while HumanEval rose 80.1 to 91.0. SWE-bench passes: 7.8% fail the full developer tests and 29.6% behave differently from the real fix.
agent_test: Report agent-written test pass separately from held-out test pass; gate done on an independent check.
audit_note: Reflexion and PatchDiff numbers match; note the SWE-bench figures concern benchmark (developer-written) tests being incomplete, not self-generated tests, so they only loosely support the headline.

claim: Generating a reproduction test and using it to filter many candidate patches gave the largest single gain in a fixed pipeline: Agentless 77 (majority vote) to 96 fixes of 300 at +$0.25. Sampling plateaus near 40 samples.
agent_test: Generate N candidates, select by agent-written repro test versus by majority vote, equal tokens.

claim: Tool and interface design changes results at fixed model. SWE-agent GPT-4 Turbo on Lite: 18.0 vs shell-only 11.0 vs RAG 2.67; linting-guarded edits +3.0; 100-line viewer beats 30-line (14.3) and full file (12.7). CodeAct (up to 20% higher success from executable-code actions across 17 LLMs, per its abstract) points the same way, while AutoCodeRover (19.0% on Lite) does not isolate an interface effect. Lite has 300 items, so single ablations carry about 2 points of noise.
agent_test: Ablate the edit guardrail (reject syntactically broken edits before applying) and viewer size at equal tokens.
audit_note: SWE-agent ablation numbers all check out (18.0, 11.0, 2.67, +3.0, 14.3, 12.7), but AutoCodeRover (19.0% vs SWE-agent 18.0%, different setups) does not isolate an interface effect, and CodeAct reports a 'up to 20%' action-format effect only in its abstract.
claim_before_audit: Tool and interface design changes results at fixed model. SWE-agent GPT-4 Turbo on Lite: 18.0 vs shell-only 11.0 vs RAG 2.67; linting-guarded edits +3.0; 100-line viewer beats 30-line (14.3) and full file (12.7). CodeAct and structure-aware search report similar interface effects. Lite has 300 items, so single ablations carry about 2 points of noise.

claim: A fixed localise-repair-select pipeline without agent autonomy matched or beat open agents at lower cost: Agentless GPT-4o 32.00% at $0.70 vs SWE-agent GPT-4o 18.33% at $1.62. This compares systems, not a controlled ablation, and SWE-bench Lite has flawed items.
agent_test: Compare a free-form loop versus fixed phases with the same model and equal tokens on our own tasks.

claim: Failed edits compound. 51.7% of SWE-agent trajectories had at least one failed edit; the chance an edit eventually works is 90.5% with no failure and 57.2% after one. Failed runs are longer (+12.6% to +82.5%) and returns drop sharply after about 25 rounds.
agent_test: After 2 failed edits force relocalise-and-restate; compare with continuing, equal tokens.

claim: Repeating the fault localiser gives a usable confidence signal: agreement across runs correlates with correctness (Spearman 0.57 Defects4J, 0.52 BugsInPy), and function-call retrieval beat Ochiai at top-1.
agent_test: Sample localisation k times; branch to more investigation only when runs disagree.

claim: Adding test-coverage fault-localisation hints to LLM code search raised AutoCodeRover on Lite from 57 to 66 resolved (19.0% to 22.0%).
agent_test: Give the localiser coverage of the failing test as a hint vs not.

claim: SWE-bench resolve rates are inflated by leakage, weak tests and flawed items. SWE-Bench+: 32.67% of passed patches leaked the answer; 12.47% fell to 3.97% after filtering. Lite: 4.3% contain the exact patch. PatchDiff: 29.6% differ from true behaviour. Fresh and private sets: SWE-bench-Live 19.25% vs 43.20% for the same agent-model pair on Verified; SWE-Bench Pro commercial set best 17.8%. SWE-Bench+ also reports 31.08% weak-test suspicious patches.
agent_test: Use held-out, post-cutoff tasks and hidden tests for any claim about our agent.
audit_note: Numbers all check; note the 12.47 to 3.97 drop is SWE-agent+GPT-4 only, and lower scores on SWE-bench-Live/Pro could partly reflect task difficulty rather than inflation alone.

claim: For non-reasoning models: fail to fix an error that sits in their own output yet fix the same error in the user turn (blind spot 64.5% over 14 models; appending Wait cut it 89.3%). Reasoning models show a small or negative blind spot (R1-Distill-Llama-70B -0.03 to -0.05 on two sets), so the colleague-framing fix is likely moot for them. GPT-3.5 kept its answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K.
agent_test: Only worth testing on a non-reasoning mode: present the draft as a colleague's answer vs your answer at equal tokens. For reasoning models, test on code first, since the 2026 data are math and logic with injected errors.
audit_note: Minor: R1-Distill-Llama-70B blind spot is -0.031 and -0.05 on two sets but +0.113 on SCLI5, which the claim omits; 'moot' is an inference.

claim: Multi-agent debate gains are mostly extra sampling: GSM8K debate 83.2/83.0 vs self-consistency 85.3 at 6 and 88.2 at 9 responses.
agent_test: Prefer self-consistency or test-based selection over debate at equal tokens.

claim: Self-debugging needs a capable base model, but the evidence is mixed. Reflexion with StarChat-beta: 0.26 to 0.26. Contrary: Chen StarCoder MBPP 47.2 to 53.2 with trace; LDB barely helps StarCoder. Newer data: S* self-debug adds +1.0 (R1-Distill-32B), +3.4 (o1-mini), -2.8 (QwQ) on LiveCodeBench; debug-gym finds a debugger tool helps Claude 3.7 (37.2 to 52.1) but early pdb can hurt weaker models; Li finds weaker models correct more of their own errors than the strongest. Gain depends on how the loop is scored and on the task, not only on model size.
agent_test: Run the same loop on a small and a large model and check whether gain scales with base accuracy.

claim: A committee that picks among diverse agents' candidate patches beat the best single agent: Lite best single 27.3%, DEI committee 34.3%, union of agents about 53%. Self-repair also depends on diversity of initial programs.
agent_test: Generate diverse candidates then pick by independent verifier vs single trajectory, equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: DEI paper quotes the union (oracle) as 54.3% for the 10-agent group (53.3% at 9 agents), not exactly 'about 53%', and the 34.3% headline and union come from different group sizes.

claim: A second agent supervising the executor's strategy resolved 22.2% of issues the single agent had failed on.
agent_test: Add a one-shot critic of the strategy (not the code) after a stall; measure rescue rate at equal tokens.

claim: Multi-agent LLM failures are frequently verification and termination problems: premature termination 6.2%, no or incomplete verification 8.2%, incorrect verification 9.1% of annotated failures.
agent_test: Count how often our agent stops without running a check; add forced verification and measure.

claim: Specific feedback beats generic feedback, which beats none, in Self-Refine (code optimisation 27.5, 26.0, 24.8; sentiment reversal 43.2, 31.2, 0).
agent_test: Compare a critique that names the failing item with a generic improve-this at equal tokens.

claim: Multi-turn tool use and natural-language feedback help LLMs (MINT: +1 to 8 points per tool turn, +2 to 17 from feedback), but RLHF and instruction tuning can reduce multi-turn gains.
agent_test: Check whether our agent's gain grows with the number of tool turns.

claim: At a matched output budget with small frozen models, re-showing the failed program does not beat fresh sampling. Blind resampling beat bare-code retry by +18 net unlocks; code plus real execution facts tied blind resampling (26 vs 26 pooled); own near-miss code and runtime trace tied a content-free placebo.
agent_test: Always add new execution facts to a repair prompt; compare repair against one fresh sample at equal tokens on tasks where the first try failed.

claim: For code, most gain from serial feedback rounds arrives in the first 1 to 3 rounds. Spider: later turns add under 0.1% (Chen); debug-gym: final few rewrites bring virtually no value; S* uses 2 rounds after seeing returns flatten; CodeMonkeys: after the first few iterations, equal-cost serial and parallel mixes give similar coverage, and a run that has already approved its wrong work cannot be rescued by more iterations.
agent_test: Set a round cap of about 3 on one draft, then restart from a fresh draft; compare against an uncapped loop at equal tokens.
audit_note: Spider paper says improvement after one turn is 'within 0.1%' (claim says under 0.1%), trivial.

claim: Agent-written tests are a good filter across many candidates when no real test exists (CodeMonkeys: random 45.8, test vote then selection loop 57.4, oracle 69.8), and a poor addition when real public tests already exist (S*: generated tests 53.1 vs public only 53.8). The best selector made the model invent distinguishing inputs and read real outputs, never predict expected output. Self-decided stopping stays unsafe (Reflexion MBPP 16.3% false positives).
agent_test: Compare three selectors on the same candidate pool: own asserts, differential inputs with real outputs, independent held-out test. Report false-pass rate per selector.

claim: An explicit first-wrong-step operator is only as good as its localisation. Trusting the model's own location hint lowered correction (GPT-3.5 26.8 to 15.5, Claude 29.1 to 12.8 on GSM8K) while raising it for DeepSeek (16.7 to 26.7, n=30). Writing reasoning as discrete steps made self-localisation more reliable and gave 20-40% lift under an oracle verifier. Reasoning models localise first errors far better than older ones (ProcessBench F1 o1-mini 87.9 vs GPT-4o 61.9, math). No code study of the operator exists.
agent_test: On bugs with a known first wrong step, score the agent's named step against the truth before wiring the operator to the rewrite; then compare rewrite-with-location vs rewrite-without at equal tokens.

claim: When the model alone decides whether to keep correcting, the loop breaks more correct answers than it fixes, under every gating rule tried (single check: 10.9% broken vs 6.2% fixed; any-of-9: 21.4 vs 8.1; unanimous: 6.0 vs 3.5). Specificity falls with each added round. Li's iterative gain (60.8-67.9%) is consistent with re-solving rather than correcting.
agent_test: Keep the first draft unless the revised draft wins on an independent check; log broke-vs-fixed counts.
audit_note: Minor: arXiv 2602.02416 is titled 'Structure Enables Effective Self-Localization of Errors in LLMs' not the title the notes give; Table 1 numbers match.

claim: An outside monitor that names a stall can raise resolution, but only a stronger or rule-based one. SWE-PRM with a Sonnet 4 monitor: 40.0 to 50.6 on Verified at about 9x cost; same-size or open monitors 30.0-38.8; telling the agent the exact action was worse (44.8) than naming the failure type (50.6). A rule monitor (repeat cycle, 5 steps with no edit) gained +6.9 to +23.5 on pre-selected problem cases, but the comparison is biased toward the monitor.
agent_test: Trigger a one-shot stall check on repeat or no-edit patterns; use a different, stronger pass; compare with continuing at equal tokens on unselected tasks.

claim: Reasoning models show little or no self-output blind spot, and non-reasoning models close most of the gap with an appended Wait. This weakens the case for colleague framing on a modern reasoning agent. Data are injected errors in math and logic, not code.
agent_test: Inject known bugs into the agent's own draft and into a fake colleague draft in code tasks; compare catch rates.

claim: For strong models, failures are mostly not localisation. In SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified, 56.9% of failures (weighted over 7 models; 64.7-69.1% for the five capable models, GPT-5 68.1%) reach and edit the right locations yet produce a wrong patch; a separate study finds failed runs still hit the gold file in 72-81% of cases on SWE-Bench Lite (59-67% on Verified). The largest single sub-type is coherence collapse (overwriting or thrashing a correct edit, 22.6% of all failures); an edit-commit checkpoint recovered all 5 bit-identical-to-gold cases (existence proof only). Wrong branch point is about 10.6% of all failures.
agent_test: Checkpoint every edit that improves the independent check; restore the best checkpoint at the end; measure how often the final patch is worse than a past one.
audit_note: The 72-81% right-file rate is for failed runs on SWE-Bench Lite only (3 agents); on Verified it is 59-67%, and 56.9% is the weighted average over 7 models (strong models range 64.7-69.1%), not only strong ones.
claim_before_audit: For strong models, failures are mostly not localisation. 56.9% of SWE-agent failures reach and edit the right function (GPT-5 68.1%); 72-81% touch the right file even in failures. The largest single bucket is overwriting or thrashing a correct edit (22.6% of all failures); an edit-commit checkpoint recovered all 5 exact-gold cases. Wrong branch point is about 10% of all failures.

claim: A real debugger helps strong models on hard repo bugs and not on easy tasks. debug-gym, SWE-bench Lite, Claude 3.7: rewrite-only 37.2, pdb from the start 48.4, pdb only after 5 rewrites 52.1. Early pdb harmed weaker models in the authors' text. Aider: no effect. Small margins in LDB suggest runtime values help only a little with simple function-level bugs.
agent_test: Offer probing only after the first failed edits; compare to read-only at equal tokens.

claim: Held-out and private sets give about half or less of public-set scores. SWE-bench-Live: 19.25% vs 43.20% for the same agent and model on Verified; repos already in SWE-bench 22.96% vs 18.89% for new repos; no clear recency trend. SWE-Bench Pro: public best 43.6%, commercial best 17.8%.
agent_test: Report our agent on a rolling post-cutoff set with hidden tests, with the public-to-private ratio, plus the check that the answer is not in the issue text.
audit_note: Minor: Pro's 43.6% (Sonnet 4.5) and 17.8% (Opus 4.1) are best scores of different model sets (same-model GPT-5 41.8 vs 15.7), and Pro's held-out set results are not released, only commercial.
